CVE-2026-18401.description:
The non-blocking (asynchronous) JSON parser in jackson-core does not enforce the maxNumberLength constraint defined in StreamReadConstraints (default: 1000 characters). An attacker able to submit JSON to an application that uses the async parser API can supply a number token of arbitrary length, leading to excessive memory allocation and potential CPU exhaustion, resulting in a denial of service.



The synchronous parser enforces this limit correctly, so the constraint is applied inconsistently depending on which parsing API the application uses.



Root cause: the async parsing path in NonBlockingUtf8JsonParserBase and related classes never invokes the number length validation methods. Number parsing methods such as _finishNumberIntegralPart() accumulate digits into the TextBuffer without any length check, then call _valueComplete() to finalize the token. _valueComplete() does not call resetInt() or resetFloat(), which are the methods in ParserBase where validateIntegerLength() and validateFPLength() are performed. Because that validation step is skipped, maxNumberLength is never enforced on the async code path.



Impact: an attacker sending a JSON document containing an arbitrarily long number to an application using the async parser (for example a Spring WebFlux or other reactive application) can cause unbounded allocation in the TextBuffer and an OutOfMemoryError. If the application subsequently calls getBigIntegerValue() or getDecimalValue(), the JVM may additionally be tied up in O(n^2) BigInteger parsing, causing CPU-based denial of service.



No privileges or user interaction beyond the ability to submit data for parsing are required.



This issue affects com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-core from version 2.15.0 through 2.18.5 and from 2.19.0 through 2.21.0, and tools.jackson.core:jackson-core from 3.0.0 through 3.0.x.



Versions prior to 2.15.0 are not affected, because StreamReadConstraints -- which defines the maxNumberLength setting -- was first introduced in jackson-core 2.15.0, so no such constraint exists to be bypassed in earlier releases. Note that GHSA-72hv-8253-57qq records the lower bound of the affected 2.x range as 2.0.0.

CVE-2026-68494.description:
The fix released in jackson-core 2.18.6 and 2.21.1 for CVE-2026-18401 (GHSA-72hv-8253-57qq, number length constraint bypass in the non-blocking parser) is incomplete. This record covers the remaining bypass.

The earlier fix wired validateIntegerLength() into a new _setIntLength() helper and invoked it wherever the integer portion of a number is decided: a terminator byte arrives, a '.' or 'e'/'E' is seen, or input ends inside a fully buffered value. It was not invoked on the attacker-relevant path where the parser runs out of input while still inside the MINOR_NUMBER_INTEGER_DIGITS minor state and returns NOT_AVAILABLE to the caller.

As a result, an attacker who streams JSON to a non-blocking parser in many small chunks, without ever sending a terminator byte, keeps the parser inside MINOR_NUMBER_INTEGER_DIGITS indefinitely. _textBuffer.expandCurrentSegment() grows the accumulator on every chunk while validateIntegerLength() is never called. The accumulator is bounded only by maxStringLength (20 MiB by default) rather than by maxNumberLength (1000 by default), an amplification of roughly 20,000x over the documented limit. Because Java char values occupy two bytes, a single connection can be driven to approximately 40 MiB of heap before the validator finally fires when the value completes.

The equivalent fraction-path code is correct: _finishFloatFraction() calls _setFractLength() before its NOT_AVAILABLE return. The missing call affects the integer-digit paths in _startPositiveNumber(), _startNegativeNumber() and _finishNumberIntegralPart() in NonBlockingUtf8JsonParserBase.

Impact: reactive frameworks such as Spring WebFlux/Reactor, Quarkus, Helidon and Vert.x feed inbound HTTP or gRPC bytes to the async parser as they arrive, which is precisely the chunked-feed shape required. Operators who set StreamReadConstraints.maxNumberLength expecting it to cap memory per number value do not get that guarantee; memory accumulates per concurrent connection and attacker-controlled concurrency can exhaust the JVM heap. The synchronous parsers (UTF8StreamJsonParser, ReaderBasedJsonParser) and the async parser operating on complete input are not affected.

Exploitation requires only the ability to stream data to a parsing endpoint; no privileges or user interaction are needed.

This issue affects com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-core from version 2.15.0 through 2.18.7, and from 2.19.0 through 2.21.3, and tools.jackson.core:jackson-core from 3.0.0 through 3.1.3. Versions prior to 2.15.0 are not affected, because StreamReadConstraints -- which defines the maxNumberLength setting -- was first introduced in jackson-core 2.15.0, so no such constraint exists to be bypassed in earlier releases. Instead, the code path re-uses the *string*-value length check, which is ~2000x larger by default. return growArrayBy(arr, more); } ``` is called on *every* growth of the name-decoding 'quad' buffer throughout `UTF8StreamJsonParser`'s property-name scanning loops (e.g. `src/main/java/tools/jackson/core/json/UTF8StreamJsonParser.java:2501,2517,2528,2540,2559,2575,...`), so an over-long name is rejected within a few buffer doublings, well before tens of KB are allocated. **`ReaderBasedJsonParser` does not.** The character-input slow path, `_parseName2()` (`src/main/java/tools/jackson/core/json/ReaderBasedJsonParser.java:1942-1993`), accumulates the name into `_textBuffer` and, when a segment fills, calls: ```java outBuf = _textBuffer.finishCurrentSegment(); // line 1982 ``` `TextBuffer.finishCurrentSegment()` (`src/main/java/tools/jackson/core/util/TextBuffer.java:990-1002`) only calls: ```java validateStringLength(_segmentSize); // line 1002 the STRING limit, not the NAME limit ``` The correct check, `_streamReadConstraints.validateNameLength(len)`, is only reached afterward, once the *entire* name has been scanned to its closing quote, inside `CharsToNameCanonicalizer.findSymbol()` (`src/main/java/tools/jackson/core/sym/CharsToNameCanonicalizer.java:474` and `:510`), invoked from `ReaderBasedJsonParser.java:1991`. By that point the full name up to `maxStringLength` characters has already been buffered in memory. This is a genuine cross-implementation inconsistency of exactly the kind flagged as a maintenance hazard for this codebase (parallel parser implementations that must be patched in lock-step); the fix for byte input was never mirrored into the char-input parser. Note also that `StreamReadConstraints.maxDocumentLength` is **disabled by default** (`DEFAULT_MAX_DOC_LEN = -1L`), so nothing else bounds the size of a single incoming token before `maxNameLength`/`maxStringLength` apply this bug is exploitable under default configuration with no other constraint needing to be misconfigured. ### PoC Empirically verified against this checkout (3.3.0-SNAPSHOT, `3.x` branch), built with `./mvnw compile`, run against `target/classes`: ```java import tools.jackson.core.*; import tools.jackson.core.exc.StreamConstraintsException; import tools.jackson.core.json.JsonFactory; public class NameLenPoC { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int nameLen = 5_000_000; // > maxNameLength(50_000), < maxStringLength(100_000_000) JsonFactory f = JsonFactory.builder() .streamReadConstraints(StreamReadConstraints.builder().build()) // defaults .build(); StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); sb.append('{').append('''); for (int i = 0; i < nameLen; i++) sb.append('a'); sb.append('\':1}'); String doc = sb.toString(); // byte-input parser: rejects almost immediately try (JsonParser p = f.createParser(doc.getBytes('UTF-8'))) { p.nextToken(); p.nextToken(); } catch (StreamConstraintsException e) { System.out.println('[bytes] ' + e.getMessage()); } // Reader/String-input parser: buffers the WHOLE 5,000,000-char name first try (JsonParser p = f.createParser(doc)) { p.nextToken(); p.nextToken(); } catch (StreamConstraintsException e) { System.out.println('[reader] ' + e.getMessage()); } } } ``` Output: ``` [bytes] threw StreamConstraintsException quickly: Name length (65536) exceeds the maximum allowed (50000, from `StreamReadConstraints.getMaxNameLength()`) [reader] threw StreamConstraintsException: Name length (5000000) exceeds the maximum allowed (50000, from `StreamReadConstraints.getMaxNameLength()`) ``` The byte-input parser's exception fires once its internal quad buffer reaches 65,536 chars-equivalent (the first growth step past the 50,000 limit). The Reader/String-input parser's exception message reports the *full* 5,000,000-character name proving the entire oversized name was scanned and buffered into `TextBuffer` before the name-length check ever ran. With no artificial cap, the same path allows buffering up to `maxStringLength` (100,000,000 chars ≈ 200 MB) per single crafted property name, from a single `JsonFactory.createParser(String)` / `createParser(Reader)` / `createParser(char[])` call i.e. any consumer that reads an HTTP body (or other untrusted input) into a `String`/`Reader` before parsing, which is extremely common. ### Impact Any application using `jackson-core` (directly, or via `jackson-databind`/other Jackson modules) to parse untrusted JSON supplied as a `String`, `Reader`, or `char[]` instead of raw UTF-8 bytes is affected under default configuration. CVE-2026-89407.description:
NumberInput.looksLikeValidNumber() in FasterXML jackson-core pre-validates "stringified numbers" with two regular expressions: PATTERN_FLOAT ([+-]?[0-9]*[\.]?[0-9]+([eE][+-]?[0-9]+)?), present since 2.17.0, and PATTERN_FLOAT_TRAILING_DOT, added in 2.17.2. PATTERN_FLOAT places adjacent quantifiers over the same character class -- an optional [0-9]* run, an optional dot, then a required [0-9]+ run -- so input that ultimately fails to match forces Java's backtracking engine to retry every possible split point of the digit run. 



Matching cost therefore grows with the square of the input length. 



An attacker who can supply JSON that an application deserializes into a numeric target type reaches this method through jackson-databind's default String-to-number coercion (StdDeserializer and NumberDeserializers for BigDecimal, BigInteger, Double and Float). 



Because StreamReadConstraints.maxStringLength defaults to 20,000,000 characters, no constraint bounds the input before it reaches the regex. 



Testing by the reporter confirmed O(n^2) growth across five consecutive input-size doublings, with a single 160,000-character string consuming roughly 74 seconds in one call; a small number of concurrent requests of ordinary body size can therefore exhaust a server's request-handling thread pool. 



The affected method does not exist before 2.17.0, so 2.16.x and earlier releases are not affected. 



The fix replaces both regular expressions with a hand-rolled single-pass scan.

CVE-2026-89425.description: UTF8DataInputJsonParser._reportInvalidToken() in FasterXML jackson-core builds the offending-token text for its error message by appending Java identifier characters to a StringBuilder in a loop that has no upper bound. UTF8DataInputJsonParser was introduced in 2.8.0 together with createParser(DataInput); releases before 2.8.0 do not contain the affected class.

CVE-2026-18401.description:
The non-blocking (asynchronous) JSON parser in jackson-core does not enforce the maxNumberLength constraint defined in StreamReadConstraints (default: 1000 characters). An attacker able to submit JSON to an application that uses the async parser API can supply a number token of arbitrary length, leading to excessive memory allocation and potential CPU exhaustion, resulting in a denial of service.



The synchronous parser enforces this limit correctly, so the constraint is applied inconsistently depending on which parsing API the application uses.

No privileges or user interaction beyond the ability to submit data for parsing are required.

CVE-2026-68494.description:
The fix released in jackson-core 2.18.6 and 2.21.1 for CVE-2026-18401 (GHSA-72hv-8253-57qq, number length constraint bypass in the non-blocking parser) is incomplete. This record covers the remaining bypass.

The earlier fix wired validateIntegerLength() into a new _setIntLength() helper and invoked it wherever the integer portion of a number is decided: a terminator byte arrives, a '.' or 'e'/'E' is seen, or input ends inside a fully buffered value. It was not invoked on the attacker-relevant path where the parser runs out of input while still inside the MINOR_NUMBER_INTEGER_DIGITS minor state and returns NOT_AVAILABLE to the caller.

As a result, an attacker who streams JSON to a non-blocking parser in many small chunks, without ever sending a terminator byte, keeps the parser inside MINOR_NUMBER_INTEGER_DIGITS indefinitely. _textBuffer.expandCurrentSegment() grows the accumulator on every chunk while validateIntegerLength() is never called. The accumulator is bounded only by maxStringLength (20 MiB by default) rather than by maxNumberLength (1000 by default), an amplification of roughly 20,000x over the documented limit. Because Java char values occupy two bytes, a single connection can be driven to approximately 40 MiB of heap before the validator finally fires when the value completes.

The equivalent fraction-path code is correct: _finishFloatFraction() calls _setFractLength() before its NOT_AVAILABLE return. The missing call affects the integer-digit paths in _startPositiveNumber(), _startNegativeNumber() and _finishNumberIntegralPart() in NonBlockingUtf8JsonParserBase.

Impact: reactive frameworks such as Spring WebFlux/Reactor, Quarkus, Helidon and Vert.x feed inbound HTTP or gRPC bytes to the async parser as they arrive, which is precisely the chunked-feed shape required. Operators who set StreamReadConstraints.maxNumberLength expecting it to cap memory per number value do not get that guarantee; memory accumulates per concurrent connection and attacker-controlled concurrency can exhaust the JVM heap. The synchronous parsers (UTF8StreamJsonParser, ReaderBasedJsonParser) and the async parser operating on complete input are not affected.

Exploitation requires only the ability to stream data to a parsing endpoint; no privileges or user interaction are needed.

This issue affects com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-core from version 2.15.0 through 2.18.7, and from 2.19.0 through 2.21.3, and tools.jackson.core:jackson-core from 3.0.0 through 3.1.3. Versions prior to 2.15.0 are not affected, because StreamReadConstraints -- which defines the maxNumberLength setting -- was first introduced in jackson-core 2.15.0, so no such constraint exists to be bypassed in earlier releases. Note that GHSA-r7wm-3cxj-wff9 states the affected 2.x range without a lower bound. The 2.22.x and 3.2.x release lines are not affected: those branches were created after the fix commit landed on 2026-05-21 and therefore contain it from their initial releases (2.22.0, tagged 2026-06-03, and 3.2.0, tagged 2026-06-08).

CVE-2026-68498.title: Delayed maxNameLength enforcement for char-backed input (`ReaderBasedJsonParser`) allows memory-exhaustion DoS
CVE-2026-68498.description: ### Summary `jackson-core` 3.x's `StreamReadConstraints.maxNameLength` (default 50,000 characters) is documented and intended to bound how much memory a single JSON object property name can consume while it is being parsed, independent of the much larger `maxStringLength` (default 100,000,000 characters) that bounds ordinary string *values*. For any parser built over character input `Reader`, `String`, or `char[]` sources, all served by `ReaderBasedJsonParser` that bound is not applied while the name is being accumulated. Instead, the code path re-uses the *string*-value length check, which is ~2000x larger by default. A remote attacker who can get a single, sufficiently long JSON object key parsed through this path can force the parser to allocate on the order of 100,000,000 chars (≈200 MB, and the JDK-side ArrayList-of-segments bookkeeping pushes real peak usage higher) before any `StreamConstraintsException` is ever thrown instead of the ~50,000-char (~100 KB) bound the API promises. Repeating this cheaply across concurrent requests can exhaust heap and crash the process (unauthenticated remote DoS) in any application that parses untrusted JSON from a `String`/`Reader` (e.g. an HTTP request body already read into a `String`), which is one of the most common ways `jackson-core`/`jackson-databind` consumers invoke the library. Byte-input parsers (`UTF8StreamJsonParser`, `UTF8DataInputJsonParser`, the non-blocking/async parsers) are not affected they correctly re-validate `maxNameLength` on every internal buffer growth via `ParserBase._growNameDecodeBuffer()`, so they reject an oversized name almost immediately, after allocating only a few tens of KB. ### Details `StreamReadConstraints` (`src/main/java/tools/jackson/core/StreamReadConstraints.java`) exposes two independent limits: - `maxStringLength` default `DEFAULT_MAX_STRING_LEN = 100_000_000` (line 67) - `maxNameLength` default `DEFAULT_MAX_NAME_LEN = 50_000` (line 75) `validateNameLength(int)` (line 613) is the intended enforcement point for object property names. **Byte-input parsers do this correctly.** `ParserBase._growNameDecodeBuffer()` (`src/main/java/tools/jackson/core/base/ParserBase.java:1169-1174`): ```java protected int[] _growNameDecodeBuffer(int[] arr, int more) throws StreamConstraintsException { // the following check will fail if the array is already bigger than is allowed for names _streamReadConstraints.validateNameLength(arr.length << 2); return growArrayBy(arr, more); } ``` is called on *every* growth of the name-decoding 'quad' buffer throughout `UTF8StreamJsonParser`'s property-name scanning loops (e.g. `src/main/java/tools/jackson/core/json/UTF8StreamJsonParser.java:2501,2517,2528,2540,2559,2575,...`), so an over-long name is rejected within a few buffer doublings, well before tens of KB are allocated. **`ReaderBasedJsonParser` does not.** The character-input slow path, `_parseName2()` (`src/main/java/tools/jackson/core/json/ReaderBasedJsonParser.java:1942-1993`), accumulates the name into `_textBuffer` and, when a segment fills, calls: ```java outBuf = _textBuffer.finishCurrentSegment(); // line 1982 ``` `TextBuffer.finishCurrentSegment()` (`src/main/java/tools/jackson/core/util/TextBuffer.java:990-1002`) only calls: ```java validateStringLength(_segmentSize); // line 1002 the STRING limit, not the NAME limit ``` The correct check, `_streamReadConstraints.validateNameLength(len)`, is only reached afterward, once the *entire* name has been scanned to its closing quote, inside `CharsToNameCanonicalizer.findSymbol()` (`src/main/java/tools/jackson/core/sym/CharsToNameCanonicalizer.java:474` and `:510`), invoked from `ReaderBasedJsonParser.java:1991`. By that point the full name up to `maxStringLength` characters has already been buffered in memory. This is a genuine cross-implementation inconsistency of exactly the kind flagged as a maintenance hazard for this codebase (parallel parser implementations that must be patched in lock-step); the fix for byte input was never mirrored into the char-input parser. Note also that `StreamReadConstraints.maxDocumentLength` is **disabled by default** (`DEFAULT_MAX_DOC_LEN = -1L`), so nothing else bounds the size of a single incoming token before `maxNameLength`/`maxStringLength` apply this bug is exploitable under default configuration with no other constraint needing to be misconfigured. ### PoC Empirically verified against this checkout (3.3.0-SNAPSHOT, `3.x` branch), built with `./mvnw compile`, run against `target/classes`: ```java import tools.jackson.core.*; import tools.jackson.core.exc.StreamConstraintsException; import tools.jackson.core.json.JsonFactory; public class NameLenPoC { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int nameLen = 5_000_000; // > maxNameLength(50_000), < maxStringLength(100_000_000) JsonFactory f = JsonFactory.builder() .streamReadConstraints(StreamReadConstraints.builder().build()) // defaults .build(); StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); sb.append('{').append('''); for (int i = 0; i < nameLen; i++) sb.append('a'); sb.append('\':1}'); String doc = sb.toString(); // byte-input parser: rejects almost immediately try (JsonParser p = f.createParser(doc.getBytes('UTF-8'))) { p.nextToken(); p.nextToken(); } catch (StreamConstraintsException e) { System.out.println('[bytes] ' + e.getMessage()); } // Reader/String-input parser: buffers the WHOLE 5,000,000-char name first try (JsonParser p = f.createParser(doc)) { p.nextToken(); p.nextToken(); } catch (StreamConstraintsException e) { System.out.println('[reader] ' + e.getMessage()); } } } ``` Output: ``` [bytes] threw StreamConstraintsException quickly: Name length (65536) exceeds the maximum allowed (50000, from `StreamReadConstraints.getMaxNameLength()`) [reader] threw StreamConstraintsException: Name length (5000000) exceeds the maximum allowed (50000, from `StreamReadConstraints.getMaxNameLength()`) ``` The byte-input parser's exception fires once its internal quad buffer reaches 65,536 chars-equivalent (the first growth step past the 50,000 limit). The Reader/String-input parser's exception message reports the *full* 5,000,000-character name proving the entire oversized name was scanned and buffered into `TextBuffer` before the name-length check ever ran. With no artificial cap, the same path allows buffering up to `maxStringLength` (100,000,000 chars ≈ 200 MB) per single crafted property name, from a single `JsonFactory.createParser(String)` / `createParser(Reader)` / `createParser(char[])` call i.e. any consumer that reads an HTTP body (or other untrusted input) into a `String`/`Reader` before parsing, which is extremely common. ### Impact Any application using `jackson-core` (directly, or via `jackson-databind`/other Jackson modules) to parse untrusted JSON supplied as a `String`, `Reader`, or `char[]` instead of raw UTF-8 bytes is affected under default configuration. A small number of concurrent requests, each containing one long JSON property name, can force allocation of hundreds of MB per request, exhausting heap and causing OutOfMemoryError / process crash, defeating the purpose of the dedicated `maxNameLength` DoS guard for this input path. Byte-stream (`InputStream`/`byte[]`) UTF-8 input, and non-blocking/async parsing, are not affected.

CVE-2026-89407.title: NumberInput.looksLikeValidNumber() in FasterXML jackson-core pre- ...
CVE-2026-89407.description:
NumberInput.looksLikeValidNumber() in FasterXML jackson-core pre-validates "stringified numbers" with two regular expressions: PATTERN_FLOAT ([+-]?[0-9]*[\.]?[0-9]+([eE][+-]?[0-9]+)?), present since 2.17.0, and PATTERN_FLOAT_TRAILING_DOT, added in 2.17.2. PATTERN_FLOAT places adjacent quantifiers over the same character class -- an optional [0-9]* run, an optional dot, then a required [0-9]+ run -- so input that ultimately fails to match forces Java's backtracking engine to retry every possible split point of the digit run. 



Matching cost therefore grows with the square of the input length. 



An attacker who can supply JSON that an application deserializes into a numeric target type reaches this method through jackson-databind's default String-to-number coercion (StdDeserializer and NumberDeserializers for BigDecimal, BigInteger, Double and Float). 



Because StreamReadConstraints.maxStringLength defaults to 20,000,000 characters, no constraint bounds the input before it reaches the regex. 



Testing by the reporter confirmed O(n^2) growth across five consecutive input-size doublings, with a single 160,000-character string consuming roughly 74 seconds in one call; a small number of concurrent requests of ordinary body size can therefore exhaust a server's request-handling thread pool. 



The affected method does not exist before 2.17.0, so 2.16.x and earlier releases are not affected. 



The fix replaces both regular expressions with a hand-rolled single-pass scan.
